The biggest and most difficult problem in the world of biology is a genetic disorder called Edwards' syndrome.
Every person with this syndrome has an inherited gene for it, but there are some who have an extra copy of a protein that helps them to grow normally, even when they're not genetically identical. The result? An abnormally small brain that's smaller than normal.
This means they can't use language or think at all. And their brains don't develop normally, which means that these children might suffer from developmental problems as adults.
"It's very difficult to get kids diagnosed with this disorder because nobody knows what causes it," said Michael Kammen, professor of pediatrics and genetics at the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine, who wasn't involved in the study.
Kammen and his colleagues looked at 108 boys with Edwards' syndrome, which can cause intellectual disabilities like autism. They found that about half of those affected had an extra copy of a protein that helps them to grow normally.
If you have this syndrome, you could expect your child to be unusually smart. But you also might find that they're less creative than usual, and more likely to act out in other ways.

The inner workings of a simple super-computer
Our first thoughts on the inner workings of a computer came from a series of papers presented at the University of Minnesota’s Center for Computational Physics. The work was carried out by researchers at the Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) in Menlo Park, CA. In addition to its theoretical and experimental results, IAS has also been used to study the microphysical world that surrounds us – the quantum realm.
The paper entitled “The Inner Structure of a Super-Computer” is published in Physical Review Letters. The paper describes the research that led to the development of the first computer that could simulate quantum mechanics. This computer was created using a combination of three different materials: germanium and gallium arsenide, which are both known as gallium nitride or GaN nitride because they have similar electronic properties.
In this article we will take an overview of what is required for a computer to perform these functions. We will also focus on some of the more interesting applications of the new technology. In particular, we will discuss how scientists at IBM, for example, are working with quantum computing to help solve problems related to quantum information processing.

A night’s sleep is essential to your health and wellbeing, but it can be even more important than you think. Getting enough rest helps to keep your body functioning at its best and helps keep your mind and body working in optimal condition. Lack of sleep may also contribute to feelings of depression or anxiety. If you're experiencing these symptoms, take action now to make sure that you get adequate amounts of sleep.

Regular exercise improves your overall fitness and well-being. Just 30 minutes each day can add up over time, so aim to do at least one hour of moderate activity every week. This will help to boost your mood and improve your circulation and cardiovascular health. You should also avoid smoking if possible. Smoking is also known to increase your risk of heart disease, so quit immediately if you have any concerns about your health.

Eating healthy food is crucial to your overall health. Kowalski's research team helps to restore coral reef ecosystems by studying the effects of sea level rise and climate change on the water quality and productivity of tropical reefs.
Sea-level rise is a major factor in coral bleaching events that have been described as a global problem, affecting millions of people around the world. Coral bleaching occurs when elevated levels of greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide) are released into the atmosphere at an alarming rate and eventually affects entire ecosystems, including coral reefs. The changing oceans absorb this extra carbon and the resulting chemicals are toxic to the marine environment.
The team focuses their efforts on understanding how the changes in ocean chemistry may affect corals. They aim to understand the factors that influence the growth of coral reefs through laboratory experiments. The team also aims to identify ways to reduce these changes in the water column so that they can be more easily monitored for future impacts.
Kowalski, who has been involved with coral bleaching research since 1970, is an associate professor of biology at the University of South Florida. She is currently conducting postdoctoral research at the National Oceanography Center, where she will focus her work on how coral reefs respond to global warming.
